terms.definition: Says what you want: a thing, or something you'd like to do.
terms.example: Quiero dormir un poco más. — I want to sleep a bit more.
terms.discussion: With people it also means love: 'te quiero' is what you say to family and close friends.

terms.definition: Means 'you' when you talk to one friend, a kid, or someone in your family.
terms.example: Oye, ¿tú vienes a la fiesta? — Hey, are you coming to the party?
terms.discussion: In Argentina and Uruguay people say 'vos' instead. You'll hear it there, but 'tú' works everywhere.

terms.definition: Says what you have or own, and also how old you are.
terms.example: Tengo dos hermanos y un perro. — I have two brothers and a dog.
terms.anti_example: Not 'soy treinta años' for 'I'm thirty': say 'tengo treinta años'.

terms.definition: Polite 'you' for one stranger, older person or boss. Its verb takes the 'he/she' form.
terms.example: ¿Usted es la doctora García? — Are you Doctor García?
terms.anti_example: Not 'usted eres' or 'usted tienes': say 'usted es', 'usted tiene'.

terms.definition: Lets you say you're able to do something, or ask someone for a favor.
terms.example: ¿Puedes abrir la ventana? Hace calor. — Can you open the window? It's hot.
terms.anti_example: For a skill you learned, use 'sé': 'sé nadar' is 'I can swim', not 'puedo nadar'.

terms.definition: Talks to two or more people at once, friends and strangers the same.
terms.example: ¿Ustedes quieren algo de tomar? — Do you all want something to drink?
terms.discussion: Spain uses 'vosotros' with friends. In Latin America 'ustedes' covers everyone, so it's the only plural 'you' you need.

terms.definition: Moves you to a place. Put 'a' before where you're going.
terms.example: Voy al mercado con mi abuela. — I'm going to the market with my grandma.
terms.discussion: 'a' + 'el' always becomes 'al': 'voy al banco', never 'voy a el banco'.

terms.definition: Goes right before the verb to turn a sentence negative.
terms.example: No tengo tiempo hoy, lo siento. — I don't have time today, sorry.
terms.anti_example: Not 'no quiero algo' for 'I don't want anything': Spanish doubles up, 'no quiero nada'.

terms.definition: Covers what you have to do: a duty, a rule, a task you can't skip.
terms.example: Tengo que trabajar el sábado. — I have to work on Saturday.
terms.anti_example: Not 'tengo trabajar' or 'tengo a trabajar': the 'que' always stays, 'tengo que trabajar'.

terms.definition: Shows movement toward the person speaking, like 'come here' or 'come to my place'.
terms.example: ¿Vienes a mi casa el domingo? — Are you coming to my place on Sunday?
terms.anti_example: When you head toward the other person, use 'ir': 'I'm coming!' is '¡Ya voy!', not '¡Ya vengo!'.
